entry.title: Go 1.27 Improves HTTP/1 Connection Reuse
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | go.dev | discussion | hacker news

The `net/http` package in Go 1.27 now automatically drains unread HTTP/1 response bodies when they are closed. This mechanism allows the transport to reuse existing TCP connections for subsequent requests, preventing the performance penalties of repeated TCP and TLS handshakes caused by partially read response bodies.

The implementation limits the automatic drain to 256 KB or 50 milliseconds to prevent excessive resource consumption. This change simplifies Go development by removing the need for manual draining logic and improves performance for applications that frequently close partially read HTTP/1 responses.

entry.title: Operating System Changes and Their Impact on Compiler Bootstrapping
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | utcc.utoronto.ca | discussion

Compiler bootstrapping, such as the transition of the Go toolchain from C to Go, relies on the ability of older compiler binaries to run on modern operating systems. While Linux's high degree of backward compatibility supports this sequence, changes in ABIs or system calls in other operating systems, such as OpenBSD, can break the chain by preventing intermediate compiler versions from executing.

The bootstrapping process also depends on the stability of external command-line interfaces for tools like linkers and assemblers. Changes in how these utilities process arguments can cause build failures in older toolchain versions. Consequently, maintaining the ability to build modern compilers from source often requires the ongoing maintenance of legacy toolchain branches to ensure compatibility with current system environments.

entry.title: antcc Fixes -O2 Performance Pessimization in Lua Benchmarks
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | 386s.org | discussion

The developer of the antcc C compiler identified a performance regression where -O2 builds were significantly slower than -O1 builds when benchmarking Lua. The issue was traced to excessive register pressure during register allocation, where over 40% of instructions in the Lua interpreter loop were stack-to-register move operations. This was caused by the mem2reg pass incorrectly generating loop-carried phi instructions for variables that were actually local to specific control flow branches, leading to an unintended expansion of the binary size.

The root cause was an issue in the SSA construction algorithm's handling of uninitialized variables. The mem2reg pass allowed recursive lookups to traverse loop back-edges, causing the compiler to incorrectly treat variables as being live across entire loop iterations. A fix was implemented to explicitly initialize variables as undefined at the alloca stage, which prevents the insertion of these erroneous phi functions and eliminates the performance penalty.
